Below is a detailed roadmap that covers both the reproduction of the methodology (how TyPro works internally) and the experimental evaluation (datasets, settings, and metrics). This plan is designed to guide you through constructing your own prototype based solely on the paper’s description.

──────────────────────────────
1. Overall Project Structure
──────────────────────────────
• Environment Setup  
  – Base your work on a fixed version of Clang/LLVM (the paper uses LLVM 10).  
  – Install and integrate a datalog solver such as Soufflé.  
  – Set up a build system so that individual source files’ fact outputs can be merged at link time.  
  – Prepare to compile and run on multiple architectures (x86_64, ARM, and if possible MIPS) or use emulators (e.g., QEMU) for ARM/MIPS testing.

• Repository & Modularity  
  – Partition the project into components: AST Fact Extraction, Datalog-based Analysis, Code Transformation (rewriting indirect calls), Runtime Library for dynamic linking support, and Evaluation harness (for benchmarks and test suites).

──────────────────────────────
2. Methodology Reproduction
──────────────────────────────
A. Fact Extraction from the Clang AST  
  • Modify Clang’s front-end so that when parsing C code, it traverses the AST and extracts the following “facts”:  
   – Type and Context Pairs:  
     ○ For every expression in a function, capture a pair (type, context) and assign a unique identifier. (E.g., TypeContextPair(n, t, c)).  
    ○ Also record global variables (as context) and function declarations (return and parameter types).  
  • Type Constructs:  
   – For pointer types, extract and store the pointee type (via a PointsTo relation).  
   – For compound types like structures and unions, record fields using relations such as StructMember (with byte offset) and UnionMember (with field type).  
  • Casts & Transfers:  
   – For every cast (explicit or implicit), record a fact in the form Cast(n_src, n_dest) indicating type propagation across casts.  
   – This should cover casts between function pointer types as well as propagations happening as parameters are passed into functions or from indirect call arguments (and return types, if used).

  • Function Pointers & Indirect Calls:  
   – Identify all “address-taken” functions by detecting expressions such as &f outside direct calls. Create facts like FunctionPointer(n, f, num_args, is_vararg).  
   – For every indirect call (e.g., e′(a1, …, am)), record ICall(N(e′), call_expression, m) along with a separate TypeCall fact that records the type expected (but note that for indirect calls the context may be approximated).  

B. Fact Aggregation and Optimizations  
  • Merge all fact sets coming from different compilation units (source files).  
  • Implement optimizations such as:  
   – Omit TypeContextPair facts that are not referenced in any other relation (to reduce the size of the fact base).  
   – Skip primitive C types (e.g., char, void) that are not relevant for function pointer propagation.  
   – Collapse chains of direct casts as described (e.g. handling “(fptr_int)((void*)&f1)” as one direct cast).  
   – Merge equivalent type/context pairs when reciprocal Cast facts exist (as outlined in the optimizations section).

C. Datalog Analysis (Type Propagation & Target Set Computation)  
  • Encode the propagation rules as Horn clauses in the datalog language. The key groups of rules are:
   1. Propagation rules:  
    – Rule (T): Transitive propagation across multiple casts.  
    – Rule (P): Pointer aliasing (bidirectional propagation when pointers get cast).  
    – Rules (S) and (U): Propagate types through structure and union fields.
   2. Target Set rules:  
    – Rule (F1) for fixed-arity functions and rule (F2) for variadic functions. These rules use the computed Cast relation to “connect” the type of an indirect call site with function pointer types that have the correct arg-count.  
   3. Indirect call context transfer (IC1 and IC2):  
    – To cover cases where the arguments’ or return types’ contexts matter, add rules that simulate context transfer from the caller to the potential callee.
  • Feed the merged and optimized fact set into Soufflé along with your Horn clause rules.  
  • Run the solver until no new facts in the TargetSet(n_call, f) relation are derived. This final relation represents the allowed function targets for every indirect call.

D. Code Transformation & Enforcement  
  • Instrument the LLVM code-generation phase:  
   – Modify or add a pass that replaces every indirect function call with a switch-case construct.
   – Each case in the switch corresponds to one valid target (as computed in the TargetSet relation) and makes a direct call using the function’s unique identifier.
   – In the default case (i.e., if the identifier does not match any target), insert code to terminate the program immediately.
  • For address-taken functions, replace function pointers in memory with a unique function identifier.  
  • Ensure that your transformation yields a binary that enforces the forward CFI policy without runtime overhead (apart from the negligible cost from the switch-case structure).

E. Dynamic Linking Support (Advanced Component)  
  • Implement module summary generation:  
   – For each module, export the “external” facts (those that might be visible across module boundaries) using additional relations (ExternalSymbol, InterfaceType, etc.) as described in the paper’s Appendix B.  
  • At runtime, build a runtime library (in C++) that loads these module summaries and re-runs the target set computation if new modules are loaded.  
  • Use just-in-time techniques to recompile new switch-case constructs when the target sets expand due to dynamic loading.  
  • (NOTE: The precise integration of the summary and JIT compilation may require further design iterations as the paper’s description is high level; document your assumptions as you implement.)

──────────────────────────────
3. Experimental Plan
──────────────────────────────
A. Benchmark Datasets and Real-World Programs  
  • SPEC CPU 2006 Benchmarks:  
   – Use the nine C programs employing indirect calls, for instance: bzip2, gcc, gobmk, h264ref, hmmer, milc, perlbench, sjeng, and sphinx3.
  • Real-world applications:  
   – Prepare to test on programs such as Apache, lighttpd, nginx, pureftpd, vsftpd, memcached, and redis (note that these may use dynamic linking and require the additional dynamic linking support).
  • Unit Tests:  
   – Construct a suite of at least 200–220 unit tests that target specific corner cases of C’s type propagation (casts, compound types, variadic functions, pointer aliasing, etc.) similar to those mentioned in the paper.

B. Compilation and Optimization Settings  
  • Use -O3 optimization and enable link-time optimization (LTO) in your build to match the paper’s evaluation conditions.  
  • Prepare builds that statically link most libraries (with one configuration also linking against unprotected GNU libc) so that you can differentiate the effects of CFI policies on legacy versus protected components.

C. Experiment Conditions and Evaluation Metrics  
  1. Correctness Testing  
   – Compare the outputs (and absence of runtime crashes) of the TyPro-protected binary against the unmodified version for each benchmark.  
   – Verify that no false negatives occur (all valid call targets are present in TargetSet) through extensive unit tests.  
  2. Security Evaluation  
   – Compute the average number of targets per indirect call:
    ○ At compile time: collect the TargetSet for each indirect call.
    ○ At runtime: implement a mechanism (or use instrumentation) to count only the indirect calls that are reached.
   – Compare these numbers against baseline CFI schemes (e.g., Clang CFI, generalized Clang CFI, IFCC, CFGuard) if possible.
   – Check that the allowed targets per call are minimal (thus reducing the gadgets available for attackers).
  3. Performance Overhead  
   – Measure runtime slowdown on each benchmark, aiming to validate the paper’s result that overhead is negligible (roughly between –0.3% and + a few percent).  
   – Evaluate binary size differences due to added switch-case constructs.  
   – For server applications (memcached, nginx, redis, etc.), run performance benchmarks (e.g., ab, ftpbench, redis-benchmark) and gather statistical averages over at least 10 runs.
  4. Compilation/Analysis Overhead  
   – Record the increased build/compile time due to AST fact extraction and datalog solver computation.  
   – For dynamic modules, measure the additional time needed for runtime target set recomputation and JIT-compilation tasks.

D. Experimental Environment  
  • Use comparable hardware setups as mentioned in the paper (e.g., an Intel Core i5 with 32GB RAM for x86_64, Apple M1 for ARM) or document your alternative if using emulators.  
  • Ensure the environment is as controlled as possible (e.g., fix CPU governor, disable CPU boost) to minimize noise in performance measurements.

──────────────────────────────
4. Points of Ambiguity to Clarify
──────────────────────────────
• The exact AST extraction details for some constructs (especially regarding implicit casts, inline assembly, or complex variable initializations) are not exhaustively described. You may need to experiment and refine how you map these to TypeContextPair or Cast facts.  
• The integration of the dynamic linking component, particularly the generation, merging, and runtime use of module summaries, may require further design choices. Explicitly document your assumptions to allow reproducibility.  
• The rule definitions for the datalog solver (especially for context propagation from indirect calls, rules IC1 and IC2) may need testing with simple examples to ensure they mimic the “target set computation” described.

──────────────────────────────
5. Roadmap Summary: Implementation Steps
──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Setup development environment (Clang/LLVM 10; install/configure Soufflé).  
Step 2. Modify Clang front-end to extract necessary facts from the AST and output them (as text files or structured datalog facts).  
Step 3. Implement fact aggregation and optimization logic (merging facts, discarding unused ones).  
Step 4. Encode the propagation and target set Horn rules in a datalog program (following rules (T), (P), (S), (U), (F1), (F2), (IC1), (IC2)).  
Step 5. Integrate Soufflé and run the analysis to compute TargetSet for each indirect call.  
Step 6. Modify LLVM’s code generator (or add a separate transformation pass) to rewrite indirect calls into switch-case constructs that dispatch based on computed target sets.  
Step 7. Build a runtime enforcement library to support dynamic linking, including module summary merging and just-in-time recompilation for updated target sets.  
Step 8. Create a suite of unit tests covering various C constructs and verify that your transformation is correct.  
Step 9. Set up experiments using SPEC CPU 2006 benchmarks and real-world applications; measure correctness, security (target set size reductions), runtime performance, and binary size overhead.  
Step 10. Collect, compare, and document all experimental results against the expected outcomes from the paper.

──────────────────────────────
6. Concluding Remarks
──────────────────────────────
This roadmap should give you a strong basis to start writing the code. Each phase (fact extraction, datalog-driven analysis, code rewriting, and dynamic/runtime enforcement) must be developed and validated independently before integration. Keep detailed logs and document any assumptions or choices made where the paper’s description is not fully detailed. This will not only ensure a faithful reproduction of the method but also ease future debugging and comparison with other forward CFI systems.

By following these steps, you will be well prepared to implement and evaluate a TyPro-inspired forward CFI scheme based solely on the paper’s descriptions.

First, we use Python with clang’s libclang bindings to traverse the C source’s AST and extract type, context, cast, function pointer, and indirect call facts. These facts will be written to a structured file. Next, a fact optimizer module will merge and prune redundant facts. The optimized fact set is then passed to Soufflé (a Datalog solver) via an interfacing module that invokes Soufflé with the provided set of Horn-clause rules (implemented as a separate .dl file) to compute the TargetSet relation mapping each indirect call to its allowed function targets. Once the target sets are generated, a code transformation module (using llvmlite or an external LLVM pass) replaces indirect calls in the LLVM IR with equivalent switch-case constructs that directly invoke validated function identifiers. Finally, a runtime enforcer component (implemented in C++ and interfaced via Python if needed) supports dynamic linking by loading module summaries and updating the target sets at runtime.
